chapter.title: Every hose on the street: Europe, 1944 to 1945

cards.body:
By June 1944 the fire is back in the house it started from. Now the hoses come from two sides at once: Americans, British and Canadians through the front door in France, the Soviets through the back from the east. **Two hoses at once, fed by factories that never ran dry.**

Picture the last day of it: 25 April 1945, American and Soviet soldiers shaking hands on a broken bridge over the Elbe river at Torgau. Between them, nothing of Germany's army is left.

cards.prompt: It is June 1944. You are a German general with exactly one spare tank division. Where do you send it?

options.text: West, to Normandy, where the landings just happened
East, where the Soviets look ready to attack
It does not matter: wherever it goes, the other side is left open

whyNot.a: That's the first hose, not the problem: send it west and the east is bare. The Soviets attacked there 16 days after D-Day.
whyNot.b: That's the second hose, not the problem: send it east and Normandy is bare. The Allies broke out of it by August.

cards.reteach: Two fronts means every soldier sent to one is a soldier missing from the other. From June 1944 Germany faced that choice every single day, and both answers were bad. That is what being squeezed means.

cards.title: The two hoses
cards.body:
On 6 June 1944, D-Day, about 156,000 Allied troops landed on 5 beaches in Normandy, France. It was the biggest sea landing ever tried. Paris was freed on 25 August.

Sixteen days after D-Day, on 22 June, the Soviets launched their own summer attack in the east and smashed a whole German army group, the largest force Germany had there.

**This was the two-front war Germany had always feared.** In 1940 it had beaten France before Russia was even in the fight. Now it had to hold both doors at once, with fewer men than either enemy.

cards.title: A bomber an hour
cards.body:
Ford's Willow Run plant in Michigan was nearly a mile long. At its peak in 1944 it rolled out a B-24 bomber roughly every hour.

A German fighter pilot might shoot down three bombers in a morning, land, and know that by the time he woke up tomorrow about 24 more had come off the line in a country his planes could not reach. He was fighting a conveyor belt. **The Allies could replace what they lost. Germany could not.**

cards.prompt: In December 1944 Germany gathers its last reserves and attacks through the Ardennes forest in the west. For about a week it gains ground. Why doesn't this change how the war ends?

options.text: The attack was too small to matter
The Allies could replace every tank and plane they lost, Germany could not, and the eastern hose was still coming
The Soviets had already taken Berlin

whyNot.a: That's the size, not the problem: it was Germany's biggest attack in the west since 1940. Size was not what it lacked.
whyNot.c: That's April 1945, not December 1944: Berlin fell 4 months later.

cards.reteach: Think of the conveyor belt. A week of German gains burned up tanks and fuel Germany could not replace, against enemies who could. And while it attacked west, the Soviets were preparing their next push in the east.

cards.title: Why May 1945
cards.body:
The second hose was heavier than the first. Allied factories outbuilt Germany in planes, tanks and trucks, and Allied bombers hit German oil plants until many German planes sat grounded for lack of fuel.

So why May, not earlier? Hitler refused any surrender, and the army kept obeying him. **It ended only when the two fronts met.** They touched at the Elbe on 25 April 1945. Soviet troops fought into Berlin. Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April. Germany surrendered on 8 May.

On the way in, the armies found the camps: Soviets at Auschwitz in January, British at Bergen-Belsen in April. This is what the war had been against.

Dev watches a D-Day film and tells his friends the Americans won the war in Europe on the beaches. His friend asks one question: where was most of Germany's army that summer? In the east. Most German soldiers who died in the war died fighting the Soviets. **If your story of 1944 to 1945 has only one hose, you have lost half the street.** Spot it by checking: did you mention the Soviets at all?

cards.prompt: A friend asks: Germany was clearly losing by autumn 1944. Why did it only surrender in May 1945?

options.text: Hitler refused any surrender, so it went on until the two fronts met and Berlin fell
The Allies ran out of supplies in autumn 1944 and had to wait
Germany was waiting for Japan to surrender first

whyNot.b: That's backwards: Allied supply was the one thing that never ran out. The factories were the whole point.
whyNot.c: That's the Pacific war, not Europe: Japan fought on until September 1945, 4 months after Germany.

cards.reteach: A fire does not go out because the house is clearly lost. It goes out when the hoses reach the last room. Hitler would not let anyone put it out, so the Allies had to walk all the way to Berlin from both sides.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: From June 1944 Germany was squeezed from Normandy in the west and by the Soviets in the east, while Allied factories replaced every loss and German ones could not. **Hitler refused to give up, so it ended only when the two fronts met:** Berlin fell, Hitler died on 30 April 1945, and Germany surrendered on 8 May.
Open a map app. Trace Normandy to Torgau on the Elbe: that is the western hose, 11 months of fighting. Then trace Warsaw to Berlin: the last stretch of the eastern one. Notice which is longer.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now describe how Germany was squeezed from two sides in the last 11 months of the war in Europe, and say why its surrender came in May 1945 and not before.
